extracted.intended_audience: poets, American writers, and readers of poetry (mid-19th-century/creative writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for poets (especially American) about subject, style, moral stance, and the aims of great poetry; a manifesto for producing lasting, authentic poetic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject: America as poetic material
rubrics_metrics.description: America and the American people are the primary and richest themes for the poet: 'The United States themselves are essentially the greatest poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'largeness' and variety of the nation—its common people, landscapes, and daily life—as authentic poetic subject-matter rather than relying only on old eastern or classical themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on common people and democratic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's highest material is found in the common people, not chiefly in executives, colleges, or churches: 'the genius of the United States is ... most in the common people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray working people, mothers, seafaring persons, early risers, cultivators, and other ordinary lives with dignity and centrality; do not restrict poetry to elites or narrow strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic quality: be transcendent and new
rubrics_metrics.description: The American poet's expression 'is to be transcendent and new'—bringing an original, expansive vision rather than merely imitating older forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for forms and insights that transcend precedent; the poet should 'turn a concentrated light' and produce work that is unmistakably fresh and original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: indirect rather than merely descriptive or epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman prescribes that American poetic expression 'is to be indirect, and not direct or descriptive or epic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid straightforward descriptive or strictly epic narration as the only mode; employ indirect, suggestive techniques that connect reality to readers' souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as the highest art
rubrics_metrics.description: ''The art of art, the glory of expression and the sunshine of the light of letters, is simplicity. Nothing is better than simplicity...''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plainness and unforced expression; avoid excess, imprecision, and ornamental clutter that stand between the reader and the thing described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial ornament, affectation, and 'gilt'
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'will not have in my writing any elegance, or effect, or originality, to hang in the way between me and the rest like curtains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce stylistic tricks or decorative effects that call attention to themselves; the composition should present its subject without visible artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and independence from custom/authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest poet 'masters' obedience and custom rather than being mastered by them; he exhibits 'silent defiance advancing from new free forms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to break precedents and invent new practical examples in form and content instead of conforming to established rules for their own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme and metrical regularity are subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyme and uniformity 'drop seeds' and may grow naturally, but they are not the essence of poetry: 'The profit of rhyme is that it drops seeds...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhyme, meter, and formal devices insofar as they grow naturally from the poem's needs; do not let formal regularity substitute for living substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision, balance, and clarity of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'precision and balance' about proper expression, and 'The purpose must surely be there, and the clue of it must be there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that even subtle or expansive poems contain an intelligible purpose or guiding clue; avoid formlessness by maintaining internal balance and clear intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as seer / visionary perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is a 'seer' with a special 'eyesight' that anticipates and reveals identities beyond ordinary investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate deep perception—an ability to see and synthesize what instruments or conventional reasoning cannot—so the poem conveys new, revelatory insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative power on the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The great poet 'brings the spirit of any or all events ... to bear on your individual character' and causes a lasting effect: 'He drags the dead out of their coffins and stands them again on their feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to alter readers' perceptions and inner life; a successful poem enlivens past and present and creates durable emotional or spiritual change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with science and wide knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact science and its practical movements 'are no checks on the greatest poet, but always his encouragement and support'—scientists are 'the lawgivers of poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on knowledge from anatomy, chemistry, astronomy, geology, history, etc.; use empirical and intellectual discovery as seedbed for poetic conception rather than seeing science as opposed to poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic moral stance and comportment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman prescribes moral behaviors—'Love the earth and sun and the animals, despise riches, give alms to every one that asks, stand up for the stupid and crazy...'—as part of being a poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a generous, egalitarian, tolerant disposition in life and art; personal conduct and democratic sympathy inform authentic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt moralizing or didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest poet 'does not moralize or make applications of morals—he knows the soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let moral feeling emerge organically from the poem's insight rather than imposing explicit lessons or preachy applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage openness and generosity among poets
rubrics_metrics.description: The American bards 'shall be mark'd for generosity and affection, and for encouraging competitors... glad to pass anything to any one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster a community ethic of sharing influence and refusing monopoly—be open to rivals and collaborators instead of guarding secrets or privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphysical and spiritual elevation as poetry's culmination
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'culmination and fruit of literary artistic expression' are in metaphysics and 'the mysteries of the spiritual world'—poetry's altitude has 'always been religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address deep metaphysical questions, mystery, and the consciousness of the future or Deity; works that touch spiritual heights are of enduring value even if 'esthetically defective.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate a unifying, divine idea in great literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing on the 'highest, only permanent ground' we must dismiss productions that 'violates or ignores, or even does not celebrate, the central divine idea of All...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that, directly or indirectly, give tone to a sense of unity, purpose, or the divine; treat literature that denies or ignores this as deficient in ultimate worth.
